title: Linear Relationships B: Graphing Lines

findings.finding: Compare graphs of the same equation constructed from different input values.
findings.breakdown: This follow-up connects the sampled coordinate pairs with the extended line.
findings.checked: p7-e and p8-part-i both graph y=x+3 using different inputs. For x=-4 and x=4, the points are (-4,-1) and (4,7), within the supplied grid.

repair.proposal: After p8-part-i, add: (i) For y=x+3, find and plot the points when x=-4 and x=4. Answer: (-4,-1) and (4,7). (ii) Explain why your graph in part i and your graph in part e represent the same line. Answer: both use y=x+3; their plotted points lie on the same straight line.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing equation and explicitly compares the two existing graphs.

findings.finding: The formulas “m=0/run=0” and “m=rise/0 undefined” use gradient, rise and run without explaining their meanings.
findings.breakdown: Students are asked to identify gradients in p13-identify, but the teaching does not connect the ratios to vertical and horizontal coordinate changes. The distinction between zero and undefined therefore rests on memorised labels.
findings.checked: All supplied preceding teaching covers substitution, coordinates, linear equations and table-based graphing. None defines gradient, rise or run. The p13 responses repeat the classifications without defining those quantities.
findings.assumptions: No additional gradient teaching is assumed; calculator use does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Beside the formulas, add: “Gradient measures steepness: m=rise/run. Rise is the vertical change between two points; run is the horizontal change. A horizontal line has zero rise. A vertical line has zero run, so its gradient is undefined because division by zero is undefined.”

findings.doneWhen: The teaching connects each zero in the formulas to its coordinate change and explains why the classifications differ.

findings.finding: Students are asked to show an intercept before the booklet defines intercepts.
findings.breakdown: Students can sketch the horizontal and vertical lines but have not been told which point the instruction asks them to identify.
findings.checked: The preceding teaching in p3–p14 explains coordinates, graphing and constant-coordinate lines but does not define intercepts. The definition in p18-definition-text comes after p16-q4.
findings.assumptions: The booklet is completed in order; intercept terminology has not been established separately.

repair.proposal: Before p16-q4, add: “An intercept is where a line meets an axis. For example, y=3 meets the y-axis at (0,3), its y-intercept; x=-4 meets the x-axis at (-4,0), its x-intercept.”

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter the definition and one example for each axis before p16-q4.

findings.finding: In the supplied practice order, inverse rectangle problems precede the direct rectangle construction that would prepare students for them.
findings.breakdown: After individual-line tasks, p17-q8 simultaneously requires coordinating boundaries, finding a dimension across signed coordinates, reversing an area or perimeter calculation and locating a missing boundary. p17-q7 supplies the direct construction and dimension-finding bridge.
findings.checked: Read the supplied practice order, including p17-q5, p17-q8 and p17-q7. Question 7 already asks students to sketch four boundaries together and calculate rectangle areas.
findings.assumptions: The supplied order governs delivery despite the numerical question labels. Rectangle area and perimeter are prior knowledge; no calculator is needed.
findings.doneWhen: Students construct rectangles from four known boundary equations before recovering a missing boundary.

findings.finding: Translate the existing rectangle and compare its area.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects changed vertical boundary equations with unchanged distances between parallel sides.
findings.checked: The original boundaries give width 3 and height 5. Moving right by 4 gives x=5 and x=2, with y=-3 and y=2 unchanged; area remains 15 square units. These equations use the topic's constant-coordinate method.
findings.assumptions: Moving four units right is interpreted by adding four to each x-coordinate.

repair.proposal: After p17-q7-b, add optional parts referring to the rectangle in (a): (c) Move the rectangle 4 units to the right. Write its four boundary equations. Answer: x=5, x=2, y=-3, y=2. (d) Find the area of the moved rectangle. Answer: 15 square units.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up retains the existing rectangle and gives the correct translated boundaries and area.

findings.finding: Use the existing graphs to identify their shared point.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a shared intercept with a point belonging to both lines.
findings.checked: The lines y=3-2x and y=2x/3-1 both cross the x-axis at (1.5,0). Their distinct slopes mean this is their sole meeting point; students can identify it directly from the graphs without solving simultaneous equations.
findings.assumptions: Students use the supplied graphs and their identified intercepts.

repair.proposal: After p19-q3b, add: (c) If the lines in (a) and (b) were drawn on the same axes, at which point would they meet? Answer: (1.5,0).

findings.doneWhen: The added part asks for the common point using the existing graphs.

findings.finding: Vary only the proposed y-coordinate to expose the comparison required when checking a point.
findings.breakdown: Keeping the equation and x-coordinate fixed separates calculating the line's y-value from comparing it with the supplied coordinate.
findings.checked: For y=2x+1 and x=2, the required y-value is 5, giving No, Yes, No for the proposed points. For x=-3 in y=1-2x, y=7, so the final answer is Yes. All steps use p21-teaching.
findings.assumptions: These are further parts under the existing point-checking task.

repair.proposal: After p23-q4-h, add the instruction “Predict before checking.” Add i “Does (2,2) lie on y=2x+1?” Answer: No. j “Does (2,5) lie on y=2x+1?” Answer: Yes. k “Does (2,8) lie on y=2x+1?” Answer: No. Follow with l “Does (-3,7) lie on y=1-2x?” Answer: Yes. In i–k, only the proposed y-coordinate varies.

findings.doneWhen: The three-part controlled run is followed by the unpatterned check, with no additional instructional prompts.

findings.finding: Connect the area and perimeter conditions for the same rectangle.
findings.breakdown: The fixed width of 4 units makes both conditions require a height of 3 units, connecting the measurements with the two possible fourth lines.
findings.checked: The width is 3-(-1)=4. Area 12 requires height 3; its perimeter is 2(4+3)=14. Both conditions therefore give y=1 or y=-5.
findings.assumptions: The rectangle area and perimeter methods used in the existing question are available.

repair.proposal: After p17-q8-d, add optional parts: e “Find the perimeter of either rectangle from part a.” Answer: 14 units. f “Explain why parts a and c give the same possible fourth lines.” Answer: both require height 3, so the fourth line is 3 units above or below y=-2: y=1 or y=-5.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing rectangle and connects its two measurement conditions.

findings.finding: p19-q1a repeats the intercept-identification task and graph from p18-a-node without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks supply the same descending line with crossings at (2,0) and (0,3) and ask students to identify its two intercepts. Expressing the answers as coordinate pairs does not supply a fresh identification task.
findings.checked: Compared both complete tasks and diagram specifications. The mathematical givens and requested intercepts are unchanged; no explicit purpose for repeating them is stated.
findings.assumptions: Both activities are completed in booklet order.

repair.proposal: Replace the graph in p19-q1a with an ungridded descending line whose intercept ticks are labelled 4 on the x-axis and 2 on the y-axis. Retain the existing response structure. Answers: x-intercept (4,0); y-intercept (0,2).

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure but uses different intercept values.

protectedGroups.observation: Each intercept is read from its own axis regardless of the signs or direction of the line.
protectedGroups.varies: The signs and magnitudes of the intercepts and the direction of the line.
protectedGroups.invariant: Ungriddded graphs with both crossings labelled and the same identification instruction.

protectedGroups.observation: Lines with different slopes and y-intercepts can have the same x-intercept.
protectedGroups.invariant: Unit grids and an x-intercept halfway between 1 and 2.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the constant through positive, negative and zero values leaves the vertical orientation and undefined gradient unchanged.
protectedGroups.invariant: Vertical orientation, equation form x=k and gradient classification.

protectedGroups.observation: The same magnitude supports comparisons of equation variable and sign.
protectedGroups.varies: x versus y, then positive versus negative constant.
protectedGroups.invariant: Constant magnitude 3 and the drawing task.

protectedGroups.observation: A vertical line's equation follows the point's x-coordinate even when its y-coordinate stays unchanged.
protectedGroups.invariant: Parallelism to the y-axis and y-coordinate 4.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the order of the terms does not change the relationship.
protectedGroups.varies: Order of the constant and x term.

protectedGroups.observation: Removing the constant shifts the line while preserving the change in y for each unit increase in x.
protectedGroups.invariant: Coefficient 3, input values and coordinate range.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the constant changes the line's vertical position while preserving its direction.
protectedGroups.invariant: Coefficient 1, input values and coordinate range.

protectedGroups.observation: The same equation supports both an equal-sides and an unequal-sides comparison, so substitution is shown to establish membership or non-membership.
protectedGroups.varies: The tested coordinates and resulting equality.
protectedGroups.invariant: The equation and the LHS/RHS substitution method.

Although the graph is reused, the response demand changes from identifying axis values to representing intercepts as points. This is not an identical whole task.

candidates.finding: p19-q1a repeats p18-a-node's whole task: identify the intercepts of the same descending line with crossings labelled 2 and 3.

dropped.reason: The follow-up requires interpreting gradient 3 as a rise of 3 for a run of 1, a connection not established by the supplied teaching. Its prerequisite is explicitly unconfirmed in the proposal. The four retained suggestions also fit the booklet's demonstrated methods more directly.

candidates.finding: Use the equation just found to connect point membership with the given gradient.

droppedQuestions.reason: The question concerns prerequisites for p24-q9, but no candidate finding reports that task's unsupported method. With c9 dropped and four stronger suggestions retained, the answer would not change a retained finding or suggestion; it therefore does not meet the context-question test.
